analysis.one_liner: Requires fuel suppliers to cut carbon in transportation fuels and blend rising volumes of low-carbon biofuels.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor: introduced November 19, 2008, 45 days before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Clean Air Act to create a national low-carbon fuel standard: companies that refine, blend, or import transportation fuel would have to steadily lower the average lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions of the fuel they sell — about 10% below a 2005-2007 baseline by 2020, with further steps after that. It would also require growing annual volumes of 'ultra-low carbon' fuels (fuels at least 50% or 75% below the baseline, mostly biofuels) to be blended into the national fuel supply from 2012 through 2025, set up a credit-trading system, add environmental sustainability standards for fuel production, and let states keep stricter rules of their own.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people, chiefly through slower growth in the greenhouse gas emissions that drive climate change and reduced dependence on imported oil — the findings section cites that 60% of U.S. crude oil and petroleum products were imported and transportation accounts for roughly a third of U.S. greenhouse gas emissions [S3]. Biofuel producers, cellulosic ethanol makers, and electric and hydrogen vehicle suppliers would gain guaranteed demand, since the bill counts electricity and hydrogen favorably and gives cellulosic and waste ethanol extra credit value [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers, climate; biofuel and EV suppliers

how_it_helps.text: Requires each obligated party (fuel refiners, blenders, and importers) to reduce average lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions of the fuel they introduce into commerce to at least 10% below the 2005-2007 baseline by 2020, and 13% below by 2025, with further reductions every five years after that.

Mandates rising annual volumes of ultra-low carbon fuels — 0.5 billion gallons of Category I (at least 50% below baseline) and 0.25 billion gallons of Category II (at least 75% below baseline) in 2012, growing to 13 and 8 billion gallons by 2025 — to be blended into the national fuel supply.

Gives electricity and hydrogen favorable lifecycle accounting that reflects the efficiency benefits of battery-electric, plug-in hybrid, and hydrogen fuel-cell vehicles, encouraging those alternatives.

Adds environmental sustainability standards — covering land use, deforestation, water quality, and protected federal lands — that low-carbon fuel sourcing must satisfy, and excludes biomass from old-growth forests, national parks, refuges, and similar protected lands.
Preserves state authority: if a state law requires equivalent or greater greenhouse gas reductions, the state law applies in that state instead of the federal provision.

analysis.who_pays: Oil refiners, blenders, and importers (the 'obligated parties') bear compliance costs and the expense of blending lower-carbon fuels; some of that cost would likely reach consumers at the pump. Corn-ethanol-heavy expansion could raise land-use and food-price pressures, which the bill's sustainability standards attempt to police.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil refiners, then drivers at the pump

drawbacks.text: The bill's deadlines were impractical: it would have required EPA to issue baseline and certification regulations by January 1, 2009 — about six weeks after introduction — even though the Congress was days from ending.
Mandated biofuel volumes and lower-carbon blending requirements raise production costs that would likely be passed to consumers as somewhat higher fuel prices.

Large-scale biofuel production carries real land-use, deforestation, and food-price risks; the bill responds by building in sustainability standards and waiver authority for states to petition EPA if supply is inadequate or harm is severe, but those safeguards depend on future agency execution.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefits — reduced emissions and less imported oil — are real but come at a genuine compliance cost for the fuel industry that would partly reach consumers, and the biofuel mandates carry land-use and food-price risks the bill tries but cannot fully guarantee away. On the whole it is a moderate, hedged climate measure rather than a dramatic one: the headline reduction (10% by 2020) is modest, and it builds on the existing renewable fuel framework rather than replacing it. Its most glaring weakness was timing — it was introduced when the session was effectively over.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the last weeks of the 110th Congress, referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and its Energy and Air Quality subcommittee, and nothing further happened before the Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. John Lewis of Georgia introduced the bill on November 19, 2008, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
The same day it was further referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality, where it stayed.
No cosponsors ever signed on, and no hearing, markup, or floor action occurred before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil refiners, blenders, and importers are better off: they never faced the low-carbon compliance obligations or biofuel blending mandates the bill would have imposed, and no fuel supplier or biofuel producer gained the new credit markets and guaranteed volumes it would have created.

for.name: Rep. John Lewis
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on November 19, 2008; no other member cosponsored it.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on November 19, 2008 and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or committee vote — before the Congress ended.

against.name: Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality
against.what_they_did: Received the referral the day of introduction and never acted on it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never attracted a single cosponsor from either party and never reached a vote, so no partisan divide was ever recorded; it arrived in the final weeks of a lame-duck session with only about 45 days left.

industries.industry: Oil refiners, blenders, and importers of transportation fuel
industries.note: As the bill's 'obligated parties,' they would bear the cost of cutting the average carbon intensity of fuel sold and blending rising volumes of low-carbon fuel, costs likely passed partly to drivers. Their interest in avoiding those obligations ran against the bill's public aims of lower emissions and less imported oil.

industries.industry: Biofuel producers (including cellulosic and waste-derived ethanol)
industries.note: The bill mandates multi-billion-gallon annual volumes of ultra-low carbon fuels from 2012 through 2025 and gives cellulosic and waste ethanol extra credit value (2.5 renewable-fuel-credit gallons per gallon through 2017), locking biofuels into the fuel supply as a regulated but guaranteed market. That entrenchment benefits producers while the land-use and food-price risks are only policed by future sustainability standards.

industries.industry: Electric utilities and electric/hydrogen vehicle suppliers
industries.note: The bill counts electricity and hydrogen favorably in lifecycle accounting to reflect the efficiency of battery-electric, plug-in hybrid, and fuel-cell vehicles, encouraging demand for those fuels and vehicles alongside the bill's public climate goals.
